hero.title: Secrets & Security: What Must Never Go Into a Repository
hero.subtitle: Why a key that has once been published cannot be taken back - and which step therefore stays with you, however well the agent works.

lead.paragraph1: The agent has finished building a small tool. It packs everything into one commit and uploads it. Among the files is one you have never opened: the agent created it on day one, and inside sits the value your tool uses to identify itself to a paid service. Nothing crashes, no warning appears. The screen looks like a good day.
lead.paragraph2: How often this happens can only be estimated, and the estimate comes from the companies that go looking: one vendor's detection engine counted about 28.65 million newly added hardcoded credentials across roughly 1.94 billion public commits in 2025. That is good for the order of magnitude and nothing more - it measures what a single program can recognize. What happens afterwards matters more anyway, because that has been studied, and the finding ages better than any count.
lead.paragraph3: That credentials do not belong in the code is something you know from the vibecoding article. What stayed open there is the question that, from the upload onwards, is the only one with a useful answer. It is not: how do I get this back? It is: what does this value still open?

bridge.title: The Sentence From the Git Article
bridge.text1: The Git article states this sentence three times: at the commit, in the interactive part, and once more as a warning. Even if you delete the file afterwards, the saved version survives. Three times the claim, not once the reason. That is exactly where this article begins.
bridge.text2: Three things the sentence does not carry, and each gets its own section here: why this is so, how far that survival reaches, and what still changes anything afterwards.
bridge.album1: You bring one picture with you from the Git article: Git is the camera, the platform is the photo album in the cloud. An album takes pictures in and keeps them - that is exactly what it is built for.
bridge.album2: What it has no handle for: taking back one that has long since arrived with everyone subscribed to the album. You can delete the picture on your side, and for you it really does disappear. For the others, nothing changes at all.
bridge.rule: So one sentence governs the rest of this article: nothing is taken out of a history. Things are only added to it.

thesis.title: What Is Actually Being Decided Here
thesis.text1: Publishing is not an action with a strong undo. It is an action with no undo - because a commit is named after its own contents, and because copies are outside your reach the moment they exist.
thesis.text2: From that follows the sorting by which you decide what an agent may do on its own: not by danger, but by way back. Anything a second action of the same kind can catch again, you may hand over. The one step for which that does not hold stays with you.

objectives.title: What You Will Be Able to Do
objectives.item1: Decide for any given value whether it is a secret - via the publish test, without having to recognize it by its appearance.
objectives.item2: Explain why a commit survives the deletion of its file, and say what the status report is a statement about and what it is not.
objectives.item3: Name what rewriting the history does not reach, and identify invalidation as the only step that changes the situation.
objectives.item4: Sort an action by whether it is reversible - and argue why that is not the same sorting as one by danger or by rights.
objectives.item5: Apply the five-point checklist before a project of your own goes public for the first time.

secret.title: The Key Is Not in the Blueprint
secret.analogy1: Some things are made to be handed on and some are not, and you cannot tell by looking at them. An architect files the building plan with the authorities, puts it up in a display case, sends it to three firms - that is exactly what it is for. The key to the finished house makes none of those journeys. It sits in a different drawer, in a different quantity, under different rules. Both belong to the same building. But only one of them is for passing around. The other is what actually lets somebody in.
secret.analogy2: Your project's code is the plan. Publishing it is normal; a whole part of this world lives on it. Publishing the key along with it is not the same thing in a more dangerous version. It is a different kind of act.
secret.definitionEveryday: A value your program uses to sign in somewhere: to a service, to a database, to a paid interface.
secret.definitionPrecise: More precisely, a secret is not recognized by how it looks but by what it grants. The test for it comes from a text about configuration rather than one about security, and it needs no technical vocabulary: could this project become public in the next minute without any access being lost? Whatever turns that answer into a no is a secret.
secret.test: This test has one property that makes it usable: it works on files you have never read. You do not have to understand what is in them. You only have to know whether access would travel along with them.
secret.ask: And if you do not know that, the shortcut is a question to the agent: what does this project use to sign in to other services, and which files hold those values? The answer is your list - and you do not have to read a line of code for it.

apiKey.label: API key
apiKey.description: A value your program uses to identify itself to somebody else's interface.

token.label: Access token
token.description: A time-limited pass issued by a service. Time-limited does not mean harmless.

keyFile.label: Private key file
keyFile.description: A file that makes a sign-in possible without anyone typing a password.

database.label: Database access
database.description: Address, user name, and the value that opens the door. The last one is the one that counts.

config.label: Configuration file
config.description: A settings file with the access built in, because that was convenient during setup.

misconception1.title: It Is Only a Test Key for a Tiny Project
misconception1.text: In the large study, the overwhelming majority of the credentials found appeared under one single owner each. So they were not sample values copied a thousand times out of some tutorial, but real keys in real use; a good 89 percent of everything found was rated genuinely sensitive by the authors. Both proportions refer to the set found in that one study. Still, the reason sits at the end and not in the number: a key does not know how big your project is. It only knows what it opens.

secret.lookLike: The second wrong assumption sounds reasonable and is the more dangerous one: I would see a password in the code. But the values in question do not look like passwords. For the same reason, every published count measures structured credentials only - the study excluded passwords because a password can be any string at all. The honest conclusion: do not hunt for secrets by eye; make sure they never sit in the saved content in the first place.
secret.analogyBreak: Ask how many copies of a front-door key exist, and somebody can tell you. A key is a thing, and things can be counted, collected, kept in one place. A digital access key is a string, and for a string that question no longer exists: it multiplies by being looked at, and nothing goes missing on your side. So the problem here is not the way back but the count - nobody knows how many people are holding it by now. What follows from that is the section after next.

ignore.title: The Ignore Rule and Its Limit
ignore.habit: The everyday form of all this is unspectacular: credentials sit in a file of their own, usually called .env; that file is not saved along with the project, and the program reads it at startup. This is not a security product but a filing habit - it just happens to remove an entire class of failure.

misconception.title: The File Is in the Ignore List, So It Is Not in the Repository
misconception.text: The manual for that list - the file is called .gitignore - says the opposite in its first sentence: an ignore list names files Git is not yet recording; files it already records are not affected. So the rule only works forwards. The case that goes wrong is therefore always the same one: the file was there first.

ignore.silent: And now the part you have to know: when the rule comes to nothing, nothing happens. No error, no notice, no warning. The file keeps appearing in the status report, but it looks like any other changed file there. That is exactly why it goes unnoticed - not because it is invisible, but because it is unremarkable. And the next collective command takes it along again.
ignore.repair: The documented repair is a step of its own: the file is released from being recorded, and only then does the rule bite. Be honest with yourself about it - that repairs the future. It changes nothing about what has already been uploaded; the earlier commit and its contents stay readable.
ignore.completion: The Git article recommends the ignore list, and that recommendation is right. What does not fit into a one-line warning is the case where the file was already there - and that is precisely the case that feels safest.
ignore.twoQuestions: From here you keep two questions apart that like to collapse into one. Is it still being recorded? And: is it still in there? Only the first has an answer on your own machine.

chain.title: Printed Is Printed
chain.intro: Your file goes into the evening edition. A year later somebody in the newspaper archive pulls that very edition off the shelf. Nothing on the page tells them that a correction ran the next morning: the correction has its own edition, its own date, its own place on the shelf. It lies beside the old text, not on top of it. A history is exactly that kind of shelf. Why it technically cannot work otherwise takes six links. Not one of them is a rule somebody laid down.
chain.stepsAriaLabel: Six links of the chain from the stored object to invalidating the value
chain.step1: An object is named after its contents
chain.step2: Deleting adds instead of taking away
chain.step3: Rewriting changes nothing, it writes replacements
chain.step4: The rewrite never reaches the copies
chain.step5: A key is a claim, not a tool
chain.step6: So: invalidate the value and replace it
chain.link1Title: Link 1: An Object Is Named After Its Contents
chain.link1Hash: In case you skipped the deep dive in the Git article: every stored object gets a name calculated from its contents. Same contents, same name. Different contents, different name.
chain.link1: A commit is such an object: the stored state, its predecessor, the people involved, your message - and the name follows from that. This has a consequence the Git article does not draw: you cannot change the contents and keep the name. The same property that makes a history tamper-evident makes it unforgettable.
chain.link2Title: Link 2: Deleting Adds Instead of Taking Away
chain.link2: That is why deleting takes nothing away. You delete the file, you save the deletion - and the number of commits goes up. The new commit describes a state without the file. The old one is untouched and still retrievable by its name.

misconception1.title: I Deleted the File and Uploaded Again, So It Is Gone
misconception1.text: Many people think this. It is not an assumption about users but what the researchers observed at scale - and the reason they concluded that the secrets remained accessible. The status report says something about the state right now. About what is stored, it says nothing.

comparison.ariaLabel: Comparison between the current state and what stays retrievable
comparison.beforeText: The state right now. The file has vanished from it, so it no longer appears. A statement about one single point in time.
comparison.afterText: Every object ever stored, named after its contents - and that in every copy of this repository there is.

chain.link3: The next thought is the advanced one and deserves respect before it gets its correction: then I will just rewrite the history. Except that a rewrite changes not one single old commit - that is impossible, see link 1. It writes replacements and moves a pointer. Afterwards the old material hangs off no branch, but it is not gone: on the machine that did the rewriting it stays retrievable until a housekeeping routine comes by - not before about two weeks, according to the manual, and some accounts put it at months. And that is the harmless half.

misconception2.title: Then I Will Just Rewrite the History, That Is the Proper Fix
misconception2.text: It feels like the expert move and it really is the most laborious of them all. It still only works where you can reach. What a rewrite does not reach is everything that is no longer yours.

chain.link4Title: Link 4: It Never Reaches the Copies
chain.fork: Two words for that, in case they are new: a clone is a complete copy of your repository on somebody else's machine. A fork is a complete copy in somebody else's account on the platform itself - made with one click, independent of you from then on.
chain.link4: Your rewrite reaches neither of them. And at this point the newspaper picture is being too kind: in a newspaper archive you have to know which edition to look in. Here the commit's name is enough. Whoever holds it gets the old state back out of the platform's cached views. What is left to you is in the platform's own guidance: contact the owners of the forks one by one. Who they are, it will not tell you.

deepDive.title: What a Forced Rewrite Does Not Reach
deepDive.text1: The platform's guidance lists it: clones on other machines, forks in other accounts, cached views from which the commit stays retrievable directly by its name, and pull requests that reference it. A pull request is the proposal to adopt a change; it holds on to the reference to the commit even when the branch has long since moved on.
deepDive.text2: The part nobody expects sits in the same guidance: you have to contact the fork owners individually, and the platform will not hand you their contact details. Support also removes cached views only where the risk cannot already be settled by replacing the affected credentials. With that, the platform itself states the order in which this works.

chain.privateRepo: That leaves the thought everyone has first: then I will delete the whole repository, or switch it to private. Both take it off the platform's front door, no more than that. Clones already taken stay, forks stay. And a value somebody has read does not become unread because the page disappears.
chain.link5Title: Link 5: A Key Is a Claim
chain.claim: And now the step that is the only one to change anything - and it changes nothing about what was published. An access key is not a tool that opens something by itself. It is a claim: I am allowed to do this. Whether it holds is decided by the service on the other side, freshly with every request.
chain.lockNotKey: You cannot retrieve the published string. But you can make sure the service no longer honors it - and then it is what it always was without that service: a string. This is the sentence from the first section, now with a mechanism behind it: when a key is lost you change the lock instead of chasing the copies.
chain.where: That does not happen in your project but at the service the key unlocks - where it was issued, in the account area. There, two buttons sit next to each other for every key: one that invalidates it, and one that issues a new one.

misconception3.title: Tiny Project, Nobody Looks in There
misconception3.text: Here the newspaper breaks a second time: it suggests a slow, scattered readership. Measured, it looks different, in two things that must not be confused. First, between the upload and the moment a string can be found through the platform's own search there was a median of about twenty seconds - that measures how quickly something becomes findable, not how quickly somebody attacks. Second, from an experiment in which a research team exposed keys of its own under controlled conditions: there are automated systems that continuously clone and scan public repositories. So whoever finds you was not looking for you. What gets looked at is everything lying open - and your project lies open.

chain.exampleTitle: Worked Through: The Timeline of One Single Key
chain.example: In the evening the project goes online; within seconds the value is findable through the platform's search. Two hours later you notice, delete the file, and save the deletion - that changes the state right now and nothing else. The next day you rewrite the history and push it up over the old state - that changes what is convenient to see and leaves every copy untouched. And then you invalidate the value at the service: the first step in that sequence that changes anything about what a stranger can still do with it.
chain.populationIntro: How often that step is actually taken has been measured - and the result is the reason this article exists.

stat.label: of the secrets found were not removed within the roughly two weeks observed
stat.description: And among the repositories observed, not one rewrote its history: what was cleaned up was cleaned up in exactly the way that removes nothing. Both proportions refer to the set found in a study from 2019.

chain.validity: That hurrying still helps has an uncomfortable reason: where nobody replaces the value, the old one keeps opening things. The same vendor whose detection engine produced the figure in the opening re-tested credentials years after they were published and found a large share of them still valid.

checkpoint1.title: Quick Self-Check
checkpoint1.item1: For a file I have never opened, I can decide whether a secret is sitting in it.
checkpoint1.item2: I can say what the status report is a statement about - and what it is not.
checkpoint1.item3: I can explain why invalidating works even though it removes the published value just as little as everything else does.

sort.title: The Step With No Way Back Is Yours
sort.intro: Before every handover to an agent there is a question, and it is not the expected one. Not: how dangerous is this? But: is there a way back? Reversible means a second action of the same kind catches the first - edit a file and edit it again, save locally and save again. The Git article already gave you this: a commit is local at first. Not reversible are publishing, deploying, deleting an account, sending a message.
sort.delimitation: If you have read the article on harness engineering, the picture will look familiar: there a key card opens three doors and not the fourth, and that is the question of rights. Here it is about a different property of the same door - whether it can be opened again behind you. The harness article asks what an agent may touch. This one asks which touch cannot be taken back.

comparison.ariaLabel: Comparison of two actions by rights and by way back
comparison.beforeText: An agent overwrites your entire working folder locally. That needs far-reaching rights and looks like a disaster - and it can be restored piece by piece.
comparison.afterLabel: Barely any rights, no way back
comparison.afterText: An agent uploads one single small text file to a public repository. That needs almost nothing - and from then on everything in this article applies.

sort.axis: Same person, same afternoon, opposite answers. The difference is not the size. It is the axis.
sort.rules: That leaves the objection: if I give the agent enough rules, this will not happen. The harness article covers that point at length, so just one sentence here - even an instruction followed perfectly does not answer who performs the step that has no way back. That question is not answered by better instructions but by your keeping the step.
sort.injection: On top of that, an agent that reads project content can also be steered by that content. What that looks like is in the article on prompt injections.
sort.doorTitle: Where the Door Stops Being a Door
sort.door: There is a moment when a door stops being a door. Before it, the door is a passage: you walk through, you come back, you walk through again. After the click it is a wall with a handle on it. The handle is still there; it just belongs to the other side now. Half a meter lies between the two states.
sort.doorBreak1: First break: you can see a door swing shut. On screen the step with no way back looks exactly like the one with it - uploading looks like saving. That is why the sorting has to be decided beforehand instead of being felt in the moment.
sort.doorBreak2: Second break: a door's lock is physics, a label is a claim. What that means for the machines standing in front of the step is in the next section.

checkpoint2.title: Quick Self-Check
checkpoint2.item1: I can sort a new action by whether there is a way back - separately from the question of rights.
checkpoint2.item2: I can name two reasons why a machine check before the upload is not a floor to stand on.

limits.title: What the Machines Do Not Take Off You
limits.gate: Machine checks in front of the irreversible step are real and worth their money. The platform's push protection stops an upload that carries recognized credentials before it lands - and the stated reason is exactly the one from this article: afterwards it would already be part of the history. For uploads to public repositories this protection is on by default.

misconception.title: The Platform Scans, So I Am Covered
misconception.text: Two limits, both from the documentation itself, and they have nothing to do with each other. First, such a check recognizes the patterns it knows. Second, a person with write access can get past it by stating a reason; that event is recorded only where the protection is additionally switched on at repository level. On top of that comes the automatic quarantine some providers apply to exposed keys: it exists, it covers particular providers and formats, and it fires after publication. Both are useful. Neither is a floor to stand on.

limits.bypass: The interesting moment is the prompt. A check that asks you for a reason hands the irreversible act back to a human being at exactly that instant. That is not an obstacle and not a formality - that is the point where the decision is yours again.

deepDive.title: How a Protocol Writes Down That There Is No Way Back
deepDive.text1: The Model Context Protocol gives every tool a machine-readable label for whether its effect is reversible. What is interesting is the default: if nobody states otherwise, a tool counts as destructive. The formal baseline assumption of the ecosystem is therefore that an undeclared action has no way back - and that is a published default, not an opinion.
deepDive.text2: The specification requires that labels coming from an untrusted source be treated as untrusted. The accompanying text from the protocol authors puts it more plainly: these labels are hints and not enforcement, and an untrusted source can simply state something untrue. The same specification therefore says there should always be a human in the loop who can deny a tool invocation. The label routes the decision to a person. It does not make the decision safe.

close.title: Back to That One File
close.text1: The file from the opening would have had two opportunities. On day one the single question: if this folder were public in the next minute - what would be given away? The file would have come up in the answer, even though you had never opened it. And on day five, a look at whether an ignore rule still does anything for it at all.
close.text2: If it has already happened, exactly one step changes anything about it, and it is not the one that feels like tidying up: invalidate the value at the service that issued it, and enter a new one.
close.text3: Everything that can be done again, you may hand over. The one thing that cannot be done again is yours.

takeaways.containerTitle: Checklist Before Publishing for the First Time
takeaways.item1: Ask the one question first. If this folder were public in the next minute - what would be given away? Whatever you name in the answer is what this article is about.
takeaways.item2: Ask the agent what the project uses to sign in to other services and which files hold those values. The answer is your list - and you do not have to read a line of code for it.
takeaways.item3: An ignore rule works forwards only, and only for what is not yet being recorded. If it fails to bite, nobody tells you: the file keeps sitting in the status report and looks like any other one there.
takeaways.item4: If something did get out: invalidate first, tidy up second. That happens at the service that issued the key. Removing the file is cosmetics - the platform itself treats removal as the fallback for cases where replacing is impossible.
takeaways.item5: The step with no way back stays with you. Editing, building, saving locally: hand over as much as you like. Publishing is a human decision - and when a machine check asks you to confirm, that question is the decision, not an obstacle.

q1.question: Two values sit next to each other in your project: the name of the payment service your tool uses, and a string your program uses to sign in there. Which of them is a secret?
q1.a: Both, because together they give a complete picture of what your project actually does.
q1.b: Only the string, because it grants access; the name of the service does not do that.
q1.c: Only the name, because it reveals first of all where there is something to take.
q1.d: Neither, as long as the project is small and is not yet earning any money at all.
q1.explanation: The test does not ask how important something looks, but what would be lost if the folder were public in the next minute. The name of a service opens nothing. The string your program signs in with does open something - and that is what makes it a secret.

q2.question: Why can rewriting the history not simply change the old commits?
q2.a: Because the platform allows changes to old commits only for the owners of a repository.
q2.b: Because an object's name comes from its contents: new contents, new object.
q2.c: Because Git stores old commits encrypted and the key for that is lost after the push.
q2.d: Because a rewrite only affects the branches, and branches hold no contents at all.
q2.explanation: A commit is named after its contents. Change the contents and you have a different object with a different name; the old one stays lying next to it. A rewrite therefore writes replacements and moves a pointer - change anything it cannot.

q3.question: Two people put the same file into the ignore list: one before the agent even creates the file, the other only after the file has long been recorded. Who is protected?
q3.a: Both, because an ignore list applies to the whole folder and not to individual files.
q3.b: Only the first, because the rule bites solely for files that are not yet recorded.
q3.c: Only the second, because an entry after saving is what takes the file out of storage.
q3.d: Neither, because an ignore list is a suggestion and is bypassed during the upload.
q3.explanation: An ignore rule works forwards only, and only for what is not yet being recorded. In the second case it comes to nothing, and nobody tells you: the file keeps sitting in the status report and looks like any other changed file there.

q4.question: An access key has ended up in a public repository, and you notice two hours later. What do you start with?
q4.a: With removing the file, so that the current state no longer contains this value.
q4.b: With rewriting the history, so the old commit hangs off no branch any more.
q4.c: With invalidating it at the service, because the value then opens nothing.
q4.d: With switching to private, because the copies already taken become worthless.
q4.explanation: Removing, rewriting, and going private change something on your side. About what the value opens, none of them changes anything: only the service decides whether it still honors the key. That is why invalidating comes first, and tidying up comes after.

q5.question: Your agent is to do two things today: rename 200 files in the project folder, and send a prepared message to a mailing list. Which of the two do you keep - and why is that not a question of rights?
q5.a: The renaming, because it affects far more files and the damage there would be greatest.
q5.b: The sending, because no second step of the same kind could catch it again.
q5.c: Both, because rights and reversibility are in the end two names for one sorting.
q5.d: Neither, because the decision lies with the machine check standing in front of it.
q5.explanation: The renaming needs far-reaching rights and is nevertheless fully reversible. The sending needs almost nothing and has no way back. The sorting goes by way back - not by rights and not by extent of damage. And a check that asks hands the decision back to you instead of taking it off you.
